This week in global logistics: Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliation on $20 billion of U.S. exports takes effect Sept. 8, CBP's Section 338 guidance bulletin is corrected after errors, the IEEPA refund pipeline tops $130 billion while CAPE's next phase stays stalled, TPEB rates hit a four-year high, and Middle East transshipment congestion spreads to new ports.

🇨🇦 Canada's Retaliation: Canada will match the 50% Section 338 tariffs with duties on $20 billion of U.S. exports across 874 tariff lines effective Sept. 8, doubling duties on American steel and aluminum to 50% and adding 15% to 50% on other goods. Importers moving cargo either direction should reassess landed costs now.
⚠️ Section 338 Guidance Corrected: CBP's initial implementation bulletin contained errors, including an incorrect drawback code range and an outdated Section 122 stacking reference; CBP has since corrected the guidance.
⚖️ IEEPA Refunds Top $130 Billion: CBP has accepted roughly $132.5 billion in potential and certified refunds as of Aug. 21, but CAPE's third phase, meant to expand eligibility, remains stalled with no new launch date.
🚂 Export Manifest Rule: CBP finalized a rule requiring rail carriers to transmit export manifest data electronically through ACE for any train departing the U.S.
🚢 Ocean: North American trade lane rates hit a four-year high Aug. 19 as Panama Canal draft restrictions tighten; the canal cuts daily transit slots starting Sept. 3, with a further cut Sept. 15.
TPEB: East Coast rates are outperforming the West Coast as congestion at Shanghai, Ningbo, and Zhoushan ties up capacity.
FEWB: spot rates have eased about 20% from their July peak but remain 60% above spring levels.
TAWB: blank sailing bookings run near 11% as carriers push new September peak season surcharges.
ISC: Middle East transshipment congestion has spread beyond Jeddah to Khor Fakkan, Fujairah, and Sohar, with waits topping a week at some terminals.
✈️ Air: North China U.S. West Coast demand softened again on ecommerce cancellations, while South China saw a modest rate bump from an AOG-driven backlog.

Five executive orders came out of the White House this week, and they hit Canadian imports two different ways.

Starting September 15, more Canadian goods land on the 50% Section 338 duty list, including furniture, paper products, and aluminum profiles. For products already paying Section 232 duties, the two now stack. Some aluminum profiles will pay 100%.

Starting September 29, it's not a tax question anymore. Motorcycles over 800cc, whey, molasses, non-alcoholic beer, and consumer-packaged beer, wine, brandy, and rum from Canada can't enter the U.S. at all.
USMCA certification doesn't help here. It exempts Section 301 duties, not Section 338.

This week in global logistics: the Senate passes a bill allowing tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas with a House vote pending, new Section 232 minimum-price tariffs on polysilicon take effect Dec. 4, the government objects to a blanket IEEPA refund order while letting narrower ones stand, Typhoon Dolphin shuts down China ports and disrupts TPEB and FEWB schedules, and record-low Rhine River water levels force cargo onto rail and road.

🌐 Senate Passes Russia Oil Tariff Bill: The Senate passed legislation letting the president impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas, stacking on top of existing Section 301 and Section 232 duties. The House still needs to act when it returns from recess Aug. 31. Major buyers like India, China, Turkey, and the EU could all face the additional tariffs, a broader reach than the last time this authority was used under IEEPA, which targeted India alone.

⚙️ Section 232 Polysilicon Tariffs: New minimum-import-price tariffs on polysilicon and its derivatives take effect Dec. 4, charging duty on the gap whenever a shipment sells below floors as low as $21/kg for raw silicon up to $100/kg for wafers and ingots. Importers can start modeling exposure now in the Flexport Tariff Simulator ahead of the effective date.

⚖️ IEEPA Refund Order Narrowed: The government is contesting the CIT's blanket order refunding IEEPA duties to every affected importer with finally liquidated entries, but won't challenge the narrower orders benefiting only the named plaintiffs. Importers who haven't filed their own refund claim shouldn't assume this ruling covers them automatically.

🌪️ Typhoon Dolphin and Rhine Drought Squeeze Ocean Capacity: Typhoon Dolphin shut down China ports last week, disrupting both TPEB and FEWB schedules and adding to yard congestion carriers are still clearing. Separately, record-low Rhine River water levels are limiting barge navigation through bottlenecks like the Kaub, pushing container volumes onto already-strained European rail and road networks.

🚢 Ocean:
-TPEB: rates have climbed since Aug. 1, with Asia-to-U.S. East Coast rates now at their highest level this year; book early and build buffer into cargo-ready dates out of Shanghai and Ningbo.
-TAWB: blank sailings jumped to 12.7% from 0% as carriers scale back sailings to match softer summer demand rather than let rates slide.
-ISC: India-to-U.S. East Coast rates have hit their highest level in more than two years amid a trailer and driver shortage limiting container evacuation at Nhava Sheva.

✈️ Air: Typhoon Dolphin grounded and delayed flights out of Shanghai Pudong, tightening TPEB air capacity. China-to-Europe rates have fallen for a sixth straight week as the EU's ecommerce rule changes cool demand, while carriers shift freighter capacity toward AI-hardware and data-center cargo on other lanes.

posts.content:
A liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) carrier just paid $4.6 million to skip the line at the Panama Canal. That fee is about to get more expensive.

Starting September 3, the Panama Canal Authority is capping daily transits at 34, down from 35. On September 15, it drops again to 32. The reason isn't a queue problem. It's rain. This hydrological year, the watershed has taken in 34% less rain than it should have, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) puts the odds of a Super El Niño by year end at close to 70%.

If your goods route through the canal on Asia to US East Coast lanes, or anywhere on the Latin America trades, your Q4 transit times and slot costs are both about to move. The ships getting priority under the new auction rules are also the ones losing draft, so winning a slot won't mean moving the cargo you planned to move.

Rebuild your transit assumptions before you promise a retail partner an arrival date. Price your West Coast alternative now, while it's still a choice and not a scramble.

Flexport broke down what's changing, why the water data forced the call, and what to do about it before the caps hit: https://lnkd.in/grashkdR

Is your Q4 plan still running on spring transit times?

posts.content:
This week in global logistics: BIS proposes expanding Section 232 tariffs to cables, cranes, and other copper, steel, and aluminum goods, new Section 201 tariffs land on quartz surface products while U.K. pharma duties drop to zero, Section 301 forced-labor tariffs draw a new state lawsuit as China unveils countermeasures, the Strait of Hormuz toll-free window nears its Aug. 17 expiration, and global schedule reliability falls to its worst level since 2022.

Section 232 Expansion: BIS proposed adding electric conductor cables, cranes, and other copper, steel, or aluminum goods to Section 232 coverage at 25% (15% for cranes and ag machinery). Comments are due Aug. 27. Some listed HTSUS codes may already carry tariffs, so verify each code against your own product lines before assuming new exposure.

Quartz and U.K. Pharma Rate Changes: A new Section 201 action sets in-quota quartz surface product tariffs starting at 25% and stepping down to 19% by year four, with out-of-quota rates starting at 50%. Separately, the U.K. pharma duty dropped from 10% to 0% effective July 31.

Section 301 Forced-Labor Pushback: Oregon and several other states filed a new lawsuit challenging the Section 301 forced-labor tariffs, joining private suits already before the CIT. China responded with its own countermeasures, citing both the tariffs and recent FCC restrictions.

Strait of Hormuz: Daily transits remain near 10 vessels against a normal rate of 88, and a tanker was struck Aug. 1. Talks continue on a maritime services fee framework, with the current toll-free window set to expire around Aug. 17.

Red Sea Blockade Widens: At least seven vessels bound for Saudi ports have turned back since the Saudi-linked blockade was declared in late July, a distinct escalation layered on top of the existing Cape of Good Hope diversion.

Ocean: Global schedule reliability fell to 63.1% in Q2, with average vessel delays of 5.49 days, the worst quarterly reading since 2022.
TPEB: capacity has stabilized around 88 to 90%; the Aug. 1 rate increase is holding and Panama Canal surcharges are spreading.
FEWB: blank sailings eased to 2.2% from 11.8%; Asia-Europe spot rates are starting to slip after their multi-week run-up.
TAWB: blanking dropped to 0% this week but forward data point to a 17.1% spike next week; confirm space now for the week of Aug. 10.
ISC: rates to Northwest India-to-USEC base ports are at their highest since the COVID-era peak as demand and congestion both build.

Air: North China transpacific rates fell again as demand softened, while Hong Kong-to-Europe volumes are down 23% year over year after Typhoon Noul canceled roughly 350 flights and the EU's de minimis exemption ended.

posts.content:
This is not a joke, but it kind of sounds like one... What is deployed on a Wednesday, announced on a Friday afternoon, and gets removed on a Tuesday that shouldn't have been deployed at all?

You guessed it; the exclusion of drawback on 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝟯𝟬𝟭 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝗖𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗕𝗿𝗮𝘇𝗶𝗹 and 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝟯𝟬𝟭 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗟𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀.

When the Notice of Action regarding Brazil's digital trade tariffs was posted to the Federal Register, there was absolutely no mention that drawback was ineligible, and so, when CBP deployed updates to the ACE validations that blocked drawback for these exact HTSUS classifications on August 12, 2026 (announced in CSMS on 8/14), like so many others, I was genuinely shocked.

Thankfully, CBP issued a correction this morning via 𝗖𝗦𝗠𝗦 # 𝟲𝟵𝟱𝟲𝟳𝟮𝟬𝟯. Here are the HTS numbers that ARE indeed eligible for drawback:
1️⃣ 𝗕𝗿𝗮𝘇𝗶𝗹 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝟯𝟬𝟭 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀: HTSUS 9903.05.01
2️⃣ 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗟𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝟯𝟬𝟭 𝗗𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀: HTSUS 9903.05.20-9903.05.84  

If your company is paying these tariffs and you're exporting from the US and/or destroying within the US, you probably should actively be exploring whether drawback is right for you. For those of you who already have a program in place, let’s meet. Is your current setup intentionally designed with what is necessary to optimize your recoveries and navigate the chaotic, on-and-off-again realities of these tariffs?

If your program runs on a legacy system that looks like it belongs at the DMV 🦥, it's time to re-evaluate your program; good enough is 𝗡𝗢𝗧 good enough in 2026.

This week in global logistics: The sponsors of the Russia sanctions bill reach a bipartisan deal on secondary tariffs, Section 301 tariffs prove harder to challenge in court, the Strait of Hormuz transit collapses to 17% of pre-crisis volume, and Houthi forces open a new front against Saudi-linked shipping.

🌐 Russia Sanctions Bill: Sponsors of the Senate bill pairing Russia sanctions with secondary tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy say they've struck a bipartisan deal on its terms, after weeks of reported friction. No floor vote timeline has been set yet; businesses with China or India exposure should keep watching.

⚖️ Legal Landscape: Attorneys say the Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies over forced-labor enforcement will hold up better in court than IEEPA or Section 122 tariffs. Separately, the Liberty Justice Center filed a new class-action tariff challenge intended to extend relief beyond well-resourced plaintiffs.

📦 De Minimis Rule: Trade groups praised CBP's rule ending the de minimis exemption, but a group representing express carriers is pushing for postal services, which handled about 8% of former de minimis volume, to face the same enforcement standard.

🚨 Strait of Hormuz Collapse: The strait has been effectively closed to normal commercial transit since Feb. 28, with renewed U.S.-Iran fighting resuming around July 9. Transit on July 19 ran at about 17% of pre-crisis volume, roughly 15 vessels a day versus a normal 88, with total traffic down about 90% year over year.

⚠️ Red Sea's New Front: Houthi forces opened a new front this week, attacking vessels linked to Saudi Arabia specifically and prompting some Saudi-bound ships to turn back. This adds fresh uncertainty to any near-term return to Suez transit, on top of the Suez Canal Authority's July 15 surcharge increase.

🚢 Ocean:
-TPEB: blank sailings rose to 1.2%, with carriers announcing Aug. 1 rate increases and expanding Panama Canal surcharges as canal draft limits tighten further.
-FEWB: blank sailing activity eased to 0% this week, but rates on Asia-Europe corridors remain near multi-year highs.
-TAWB: blank sailings jumped to 6.9% from 0%, with carriers announcing rate increases for early-to-mid August despite the seasonal summer lull.
-ISC: capacity stays tight with rates at a multi-year high; two direct services have resumed standard Suez routing, cutting a week of transit time.

✈️ Air: high ambient temperatures are cutting payload capacity across North China flights, tightening effective capacity independent of demand. South China's U.S. West Coast space is fully booked after a single 100-plus-ton multi-carrier booking, while Hong Kong-to-Europe volumes fell for a fifth straight week on the EU's ecommerce rule change.

posts.content:
Tomorrow morning, the U.S. tariff landscape shifts again, and this time it's built to stay. 

Today, USTR announced final action in its Section 301 forced-labor investigations: tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on 60 economies that together make up about 99% of what the U.S. imports. So nearly everyone is in scope. They take effect at 12:01am ET on July 24, the moment the temporary 10% global tariff expires.

If you import into the U.S., the good news is your landed costs probably won't jump much on day one. Most goods just move from a temporary 10% to a permanent 10% or 12.5%.

Unlike the stopgap it replaces, this action runs on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which trade attorneys consider more likely to hold up in court. Once these duties are in place, they can stay for years.
Three things worth doing now:
Map your exposure by country and product. The gap between 10% and 12.5% is real at scale, and an exemption can matter more than the headline rate.
Plan for permanence, through sourcing decisions, consolidation, and duty mitigation.

Watch what's next: more tariff actions are planned, and country rates will keep shifting as forced-labor laws change.

🚨 Section 338 Tariffs on Canada: The proposed 50% tariff, covering roughly 5% of Canadian exports to the U.S., faces an Aug. 19 deadline with only muted Republican pushback so far. Legal scholars broadly expect importers to sue if it takes effect. Importers with Canadian exposure should model both the tariff and a narrowed-retaliation scenario now.
⚠️ NFTC Flags Russia Sanctions Bill: NFTC raised concerns to Congress about the tariff mechanics in the pending Senate bill pairing Russia sanctions with secondary tariffs of up to 100% on countries like China and India. Business pushback often reshapes how broadly this kind of language gets scoped before a floor vote.
🚨 Strait of Hormuz Escalation: The corridor has reverted fully to war conditions after a new round of large-scale U.S.-Iran strikes. Weekly transits collapsed to 53 through July 20, down 66% from 157 the week before, with tanker and gas carrier crossings falling from 90 to 30.
⚠️ Red Sea Blockade Threat: On July 20, Houthi forces declared a maritime blockade targeting Saudi-linked shipping in retaliation for a blockade of Yemen and a strike on Sanaa's airport. Industry reporting flags a real risk the Bab el-Mandeb could close entirely, a material escalation beyond the existing Cape of Good Hope diversions.

🚢 Ocean:
-TPEB: blank sailings ticked up to 1.3%; rates that hit a nearly two-year high in early July are softening, but carriers have announced Aug. 1 GRIs, especially on the West Coast.
-FEWB: carriers have withdrawn 5% of scheduled sailings across major East-West trades through Week 34; demand is skewing toward the Mediterranean as Northern Europe cools under new EU ecommerce rules.
-TAWB: blank sailings jumped to 6.9% from 0% last week; Northern Europe port congestion continues with Rotterdam barge waits of 90 to 96 hours.
-ISC: capacity remains the tightest since summer 2024 as two Northwest India-to-USEC services are removed; demand is up roughly 40% since April and rates have hit an 18-month high.

✈️ Air: worldwide air cargo rates softened for a third straight week, the first back-to-back decline since February. Jet fuel remains about 38% above year-ago levels, and renewed U.S.-Iran fighting is pushing several carriers to file new fuel surcharges, with SWISS WorldCargo raising its U.S.-origin surcharge effective Aug. 3.

This week in global logistics: a draft Senate bill proposes up to 100% secondary tariffs on China and India over Russian energy purchases, DOJ opens a new trade enforcement unit, Section 301 tariffs on Brazil take effect July 22, the Strait of Hormuz closes to commercial transit amid renewed U.S.-Iran conflict, container freight rates climb for a fifth straight week, and more.

⚠️ Russia Sanctions Bill: A draft Senate bill introduced July 14 pairs new Russia sanctions with secondary tariffs of up to 100% on China and India for continued purchases of Russian oil and gas. The bill is still in draft form with no finalized scope or effective date. Importers sourcing from China or India should stress-test landed costs now.

⚖️ DOJ Trade Enforcement Expansion: DOJ added a new trade enforcement unit and published guidance on duty evasion, undervaluation, and transshipment schemes. Importers should revisit compliance controls before this expanded scrutiny arrives.

🇧🇷 Section 301 Tariffs on Brazil: A 25% tariff on Brazilian-origin goods takes effect July 22 and stacks with the existing 10% Section 122 duty until Section 122 expires July 24, after which the 25% rate remains alone. An in-transit provision covers goods that departed before July 22 and clear customs by July 29.

🚨 Strait of Hormuz Closure: Renewed U.S.-Iran conflict has closed the Strait of Hormuz to normal commercial transit since July 10. Vessel transits are down roughly 60% week over week, with about 200k TEU of capacity now restricted or trapped in the region, and one container ship was disabled by fire during an attack.

🚢 Ocean: Global container rates have risen for five straight weeks, up 9% week over week as of July 2, with Asia-U.S. West Coast spot rates up roughly 120% since mid-May.

TPEB: blank sailings dropped to 0.4%; the planned July 15 West Coast rate increase has been scaled back as capacity expands.

FEWB: blanking held at 8.8% on continued Cape of Good Hope routing; rates have peaked and are stabilizing.

TAWB: vessel utilization tops 93% across Northern Europe and West Mediterranean, with container and chassis shortages persisting across Germany, Benelux, Austria, Hungary, and Slovakia.

ISC: weekly direct ISC-to-USEC services drop from 6 to 4 by August 1 as ONE ends its WIN service, with capacity at its tightest since Summer 2024.

✈️ Air: North China demand contracted on both China-U.S. and China-Europe lanes, with the EU's new July 1 handling charge on low-value imports structurally cutting ecommerce parcel volumes to Europe. Middle East capacity recovery had narrowed to a 10% deficit versus pre-war levels, but renewed U.S.-Iran fighting risks reversing that trend.
